source_text: Iustitiam ergo primo iudicis dispice; cuius si ratio constiterit, tunc et seueritas et per quae seueritas decurrit rationi et iustitiae reputabuntur. ac ne pluribus inmoremur, adserite causas [ceteras] quoque, ut sententias condemnetis, excusate delicta, ut iudicia reprobetis. nolite reprehendere iudicem, sed reuincite malum iudicem. nam et si patrum delicta de filiis exigebat, duritia populi talia remedia compulerat, ut uel posteritatibus suis prospicientes legi diuinae oboedirent. quis enim non magis filiorum salutem quam suam curet? sed et si benedictio patrum semini quoque eorum destinabatur, sine ullo adhuc merito eius, cur non et reatus patrum in filios quoque redundaret, [sicut gratia, ita et offensa] ut per totum genus et gratia decurreret et offensa? saluo eo, quod postea decerni habebat: non dicturos acidam uuam patres manducasse et filiorum dentes obstipuisse, id est non sumpturum patrem delictum filii nec filium delictum patris, sed unumquemque delicti sui reum futurum, ut post duritiam populi duritia legis edomita iustitia iam non genus, sed personas iudicaret. quamquam si euangelium ueritatis accipias, ad quos pertineat sententia reddentis in filios patrum delicta cognosces, ad illos scilicet, qui hanc ultro sibi sententiam fuerant inrogaturi: sanguis illius super capita nostra et filiorum nostrorum. hoc itaque homini prouidentia dei censuit, quod iam audierat.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore first consider the justice of the judge; if his reason is established, then also his severity and the things through which his severity runs will be reckoned to reason and justice. And lest we linger on many things, state also the other causes, so that you may condemn the opinions, excuse the offenses, so that you may disapprove the judgments. Do not find fault with the judge, but overcome the evil judge. For even if He demanded the offenses of the fathers from the sons, the hardness of the people had compelled such remedies, so that looking ahead to their posterity they might obey the divine law. For who does not care more for the salvation of his sons than his own? But even if the blessing of the fathers was destined also for their seed, without any merit of theirs, why should not also the guilt of the fathers overflow into the sons, just as the favor, so also the offense, so that through the whole race both favor and offense might run? Except for that which was to be decided afterwards: they will not say, our fathers ate sour grapes and the teeth of our sons were set on edge, that is, the father will not take on the offense of the son, nor the son the offense of the father, but each one will be liable for his own offense, so that after the hardness of the people the hardness of the law having been overcome, justice would now judge not the race, but persons. Although if you accept the gospel of truth, you will know to whom the opinion belongs, of rendering the offenses of the fathers into the sons: the blood of that one upon our heads and our sons. Therefore God's providence decided this for man, which he had already heard.

pass_b_english: To understand the justice of a judge, you first need to examine the reasoning behind their judgments. If their reasoning holds up, then their severity and the actions that follow from it can be seen as reasonable and just. Let's not get bogged down in details - present all the relevant factors so you can assess the opinions, excuse the mistakes, and critique the judgments. Don't criticize the judge; instead, overcome the evil that's driving their judgments. Even if God demanded that children pay for their parents' sins, it was the people's stubbornness that led to such harsh measures, intended to make them obey God's law for the sake of their descendants. After all, who wouldn't prioritize their children's well-being over their own? And while the blessings of the parents were meant to extend to their children, even without them earning it, why shouldn't the parents' guilt also affect their children, just like their favor does? This would mean that both the benefits and the consequences would be passed down through the generations. However, there was a crucial exception to this rule, one that would be established later: each person would be accountable for their own actions, not their parents' (Ezekiel 18:2). This means that after the people's hardness was overcome by the law's severity, justice would focus on individual responsibility, not collective guilt. If you accept the true gospel, you'll see that the idea of children suffering for their parents' sins applies to those who chose to bring that judgment on themselves, saying, 'His blood is on us and on our children' - a decision that God's providence had already taken into account, as He had previously made clear.

review.notes: Pass B introduces a scripture citation (Ezekiel 18:2) that is not present in the Locked Latin source. While the Latin text alludes to the proverb ('non dicturos acidam uuam patres manducasse...'), the citation is an addition to the translation. Furthermore, Pass B's translation of 'sanguis illius super capita nostra et filiorum nostrorum' as 'His blood is on us and on our children' is a significant departure from the literal sense of the Latin 'the blood of that one upon our heads and our sons' provided in Pass A, though the primary failure is the unsupplied citation.
reasons: Pass B adds a scripture citation '(Ezekiel 18:2)' which is not in the Locked Latin source. The source contains the proverb 'non dicturos acidam uuam patres manducasse et filiorum dentes obstipuisse', but does not provide the citation.
